title: AQA GCSE Chemistry · Rates and Equilibrium

items.stem: A student follows the reaction between marble chips and dilute hydrochloric acid, which gives off carbon dioxide. Which set of measurements would allow the mean rate of reaction to be worked out?

options.text: The volume of gas collected, together with the time taken to collect it
The total volume of gas given off at the end, and nothing else
The time taken until the fizzing finally stops, and nothing more
The temperature of the mixture, measured every ten seconds

items.why: The rate of a chemical reaction can be found by measuring the quantity of product formed over time, so a quantity and a time are both needed.

items.stem: The specification states how the quantity of a reactant or product may be measured. Which pair does it give?

options.text: The concentration in mol/dm³ or the temperature in °C
The mass in grams or the total time taken in seconds
The volume in cm³ or the pressure of the gas in pascals
The mass measured in grams or the volume in cm³

items.why: The quantity of reactant or product can be measured by the mass in grams or by a volume in cm³ .

items.stem: Which of these is given in the specification as a unit of rate of reaction?

options.text: s/cm³
cm³ /s
mol/dm³
cm³

items.why: The units of rate of reaction may be given as g/s or cm³ /s.

items.stem: (HT) In a Higher Tier question the quantity of a reactant is given in moles. In which unit should the rate of reaction then be given?

options.text: mol/dm³
s /mol
mol
mol/s

items.why: For the Higher Tier, units for rate of reaction may be given in mol/s.

items.stem: Which list contains only factors that the specification says affect the rate of a chemical reaction?

options.text: Concentration, pressure of gases, surface area, temperature, time
Concentration, pressure of gases, surface area, temperature, catalysts
Concentration, colour of the reactants, temperature, stirring, catalysts
Concentration, pressure of gases, surface area, pH, volume of flask

items.why: This is exactly the list the specification gives.

items.stem: A reaction mixture is cooled from 40 °C to 20 °C. What happens to the rate of the reaction?

options.text: It increases, because cooling packs the particles closer together
It decreases, as collisions are less frequent and less energetic
It is unchanged, since temperature affects only the final amount made
It decreases, but only if a catalyst is taken out as well

items.why: Students should be able to recall that lowering the temperature lowers the rate.

items.stem: Required practical 5 investigates how changes in concentration affect the rate of reaction. Which pair of methods does the specification require?

options.text: Measuring the volume of a gas, and following the temperature rise in the flask
Measuring the volume of a gas, and following a colour change or turbidity
Measuring the temperature rise, and following a colour change or turbidity
Weighing the solid left behind, and following the volume of the solution used

items.why: These are the two methods named in Required practical 5.

items.stem: What is meant by the activation energy of a reaction?

options.text: The energy given out as the products are formed
The energy that is given out when the particles collide and react
The minimum energy that particles must have in order to react
The total energy needed to make all the particles react

items.why: This is the specification's definition of activation energy.

items.stem: Which statement about catalysts is correct?

options.text: A catalyst is used up slowly, so more must be added as it goes
One catalyst will speed up any reaction that it is added to
A catalyst changes the rate of a reaction but is not used up by it
A catalyst makes a reaction produce more of the product

items.why: Catalysts change the rate of chemical reactions but are not used up during the reaction.

items.stem: A graph of the volume of gas produced against time is steep at first and then becomes less steep. What does this shape show?

options.text: The volume of gas begins to fall once the curve bends over
The reaction speeds up steadily as more product forms
The reaction runs at one steady rate the whole way
The reaction is fastest at the start, and then slows down

items.why: Steepness of the curve is a measure of rate, so a falling steepness means a falling rate.

items.stem: The line on a graph of volume of gas against time becomes horizontal after 80 s. What does this tell you?

options.text: No more gas is being made, so the reaction has ended
Gas is now being made at a steady, constant rate
The reaction is still speeding up, but more gradually
The gas is now being used up again in a reverse reaction

items.why: A horizontal line has zero gradient, so the rate is zero and the reaction has stopped.

items.stem: Required practical 5 should involve developing a hypothesis. Which of these is a suitable hypothesis for the investigation?

options.text: The higher the concentration of the acid, the faster gas will be produced
Measure the volume of gas every ten seconds for each concentration used
Add the acid to the magnesium and time each reaction with a stopwatch
Concentration and rate of reaction are connected in some way

items.why: It is a testable prediction linking the independent variable to the dependent variable.

items.stem: According to collision theory, when can a reaction between two particles take place?

options.text: Whenever they collide, no matter how gently they hit each other
Only when the collision itself gives out enough energy
Only when they collide with at least the activation energy
Whenever they are in the same container as each other

items.why: Reactions can occur only when reacting particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy.

items.stem: Why does increasing the concentration of hydrochloric acid increase the rate of its reaction with magnesium?

options.text: The acid particles move faster, so their collisions carry more energy
The activation energy of the reaction is lowered by the extra acid
More particles in the same volume means more frequent collisions
Each single collision becomes much more likely to end in a reaction

items.why: Increasing the concentration of reactants in solution increases the frequency of collisions.

items.stem: Why does raising the temperature increase the rate of a reaction? Give the full reason.

options.text: Collisions are more frequent, and that is the whole of the reason why
Collisions happen more often, and nothing else about them changes
The activation energy of the reaction falls as it is heated
Collisions are more frequent and more of them are energetic enough

items.why: Increasing the temperature increases the frequency of collisions and makes the collisions more energetic.

items.stem: Two gases react together. Why does increasing the pressure of the gases increase the rate of reaction?

options.text: Squeezing the particles closer together makes each collision harder
Raising the pressure lowers the energy that a successful collision needs
There are more gas particles present than there were before
The particles are in a smaller volume, so they collide more often

items.why: Increasing the pressure of reacting gases increases the frequency of collisions.

items.stem: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a chemical reaction?

options.text: It provides a different pathway with a lower activation energy
It lowers the activation energy of the original reaction pathway
It speeds up any reaction at all, as catalysts always do
It makes the reaction produce more product, so it goes faster

items.why: This is the specification's explanation of catalytic action.

items.stem: On a reaction profile for a catalysed reaction, how does the catalysed curve differ from the uncatalysed one?

options.text: Its hump is lower, and the reactants and products are unchanged
Its hump is lower, and the products end up at a lower energy too
Its hump is lower, and it makes more product as well
The hump is the same, but the curve reaches products sooner

items.why: The lower hump shows the lower activation energy of the new pathway; the energy levels stay the same.

items.stem: In a reaction, 3.6 g of magnesium ribbon is used up in 180 s. What is the mean rate of reaction?

options.text: 0.020 g/min
50 g/s

items.why: mean rate of reaction = (quantity of reactant used) / (time taken) = 3.6 g / 180 s.

items.stem: A gas syringe collects 12 cm³ of gas in 8 s. What is the mean rate of reaction?

options.text: 0.67 cm³ /s
1.5 cm³ /min
1.5 cm³ /s
96 cm³ /s

items.why: mean rate of reaction = (quantity of product formed) / (time taken) = 12 cm³ / 8 s.

items.stem: (HT) In a reaction, 0.60 mol of hydrogen is produced in 30 s. What is the mean rate of reaction?

options.text: 0.020 mol/min
0.020 mol/s
18 mol/s

items.why: 0.60 mol divided by 30 s, with the rate given in mol/s as the Higher Tier requires.

items.stem: A flask of reacting mixture stands on a balance. The mass falls from 82.50 g to 81.90 g in 120 s. What is the mean rate of reaction?
items.why: The mass lost is 0.60 g, and 0.60 g divided by 120 s gives 0.0050 g/s.

items.stem: Experiment X produces 30 cm³ of gas in 20 s. Experiment Y produces 45 cm³ of gas in 45 s. Which statement about the mean rates is correct?

options.text: Y is faster, because Y produces the larger total volume of gas
Y is faster, because the reaction in Y was allowed to run for longer
The mean rates are equal, since both experiments make gas steadily
X is faster: its mean rate is 1.5 cm³ /s and the mean rate of Y is 1.0 cm³ /s

items.why: Each quantity is divided by its own time before the two are compared.

items.stem: A student needs the rate of reaction at 30 s from a curved graph of volume of gas against time. What should the student do?

options.text: Draw a tangent at 30 s and work out its slope
Read the volume off the curve at 30 s and use that
Join the origin to the point at 30 s and use that slope
Divide the final volume by the total time of the run

items.why: The specification requires a tangent to be drawn and its slope used as a measure of the rate.

items.stem: (HT) A tangent drawn to a volume-time curve at 20 s passes through the points (10 s, 12 cm³ ) and (30 s, 52 cm³ ). What is the rate of reaction at 20 s?

options.text: 2.0 cm³ /s
0.50 cm³ /s
40 cm³ /s
2.0 cm³

items.why: The gradient is (52 - 12) cm³ divided by (30 - 10) s = 40 / 20 = 2.0 cm³ /s.

items.stem: A 5 g strip of magnesium and 5 g of magnesium powder are added to separate beakers of the same acid. Why does the powder react faster?

options.text: There is simply more magnesium in the powder than in the strip
It has a larger surface area to volume ratio, so collisions are more frequent
The powder particles move faster, so the collisions are more energetic
The powder must lower the activation energy needed by the reaction

items.why: The effect of the size of the pieces is explained in terms of surface area to volume ratio.

items.stem: Doubling the concentration of a solution roughly doubles the rate of reaction. Using simple ideas about proportionality, what should halving the concentration do?

options.text: Cut the rate to a quarter, since the rate depends on the square
Cut the rate by more than half, as the particles also move slower
Leave the rate unchanged, since the same amount of acid still reacts
Roughly halve the rate, as collisions become half as frequent

items.why: Simple proportionality: half the particles in the same volume gives about half the collision frequency.

items.stem: The equation for a reaction is 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂. A solid is added to the flask, the reaction speeds up, and the solid is recovered unchanged at the end. What is the solid?

options.text: A reactant, because it was added to the flask before the reaction started
A catalyst, as it speeds the reaction up and is not in the equation
A product, because it was there in the flask at the end of the reaction
An enzyme, because it is a solid substance that speeds the reaction up

items.why: Catalysts are identified from their effect on the rate and from their absence from the chemical equation.

items.stem: Which statement describes what makes a reaction a reversible reaction?

options.text: The products of the reaction can react to produce the original reactants
The reaction goes fully forwards and then it goes fully backwards
The reaction finishes with equal amounts of reactants and products
The reaction can be made faster or slower by a change of conditions

items.why: This is the definition given in the specification: in some chemical reactions the products can react to produce the original reactants.

items.stem: A reversible reaction is represented as A + B ⇌ C + D. What does the ⇌ symbol tell you?

options.text: That the mixture holds equal amounts of A, B, C and D throughout it
That the reaction can go in the forward and the reverse direction
That the mixture has already reached equilibrium at every moment
That the forward reaction is faster than the reverse reaction

items.why: The double arrow is the way the specification represents a reversible reaction: A and B can form C and D, and C and D can form A and B.

items.stem: The forward reaction of a reversible reaction is exothermic. What can be said about the reverse reaction?

options.text: It is exothermic as well and transfers the same amount of energy back
It is endothermic and transfers the same amount of energy as the forward one
It is endothermic but it transfers less energy than the forward one
It is endothermic and the energy transferred depends on the rate

items.why: If a reversible reaction is exothermic in one direction it is endothermic in the opposite direction, and the same amount of energy is transferred.

items.stem: A reversible reaction takes place in a sealed flask. When is the mixture at equilibrium?

options.text: When both the forward and the reverse reactions have completely stopped
When the amounts of all the reactants and of all the products are the same
When all of the reactants have been converted into the products
When the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate

items.why: This is the specification's definition of equilibrium in apparatus which prevents the escape of reactants and products.

items.stem: The same reversible reaction is allowed to reach equilibrium at two different temperatures. What can be said about the amounts of the substances present?

options.text: The amounts must be equal at equilibrium whatever conditions are used
The amounts depend only on how quickly equilibrium was reached
The relative amounts of the reactants and products depend on the conditions
The amounts are fixed by the masses that were mixed at the start

items.why: The specification states that the relative amounts of all the reactants and products at equilibrium depend on the conditions of the reaction.

items.stem: A system at equilibrium has one of its conditions changed. According to the specification, how does the system respond?

options.text: It responds until the change made to it has been cancelled out completely
It stays exactly as it was, because it is already at equilibrium
It stops reacting until the original conditions are restored
It responds in the direction that counteracts the change that was made

items.why: If a system at equilibrium has a condition changed, the system responds to counteract the change.

items.stem: What can Le Chatelier's Principle be used for?

options.text: Predicting the effect of changing conditions on a system at equilibrium
Calculating the exact amount of each product present at the new equilibrium
Predicting how long a given mixture will take to reach equilibrium again
Showing that heating a reaction always increases its yield

items.why: The effects of changing conditions on a system at equilibrium can be predicted using Le Chatelier's Principle.

items.stem: The concentration of one substance in a mixture at equilibrium is changed. What happens to the concentrations of the other substances?

options.text: Only the substance whose concentration was altered is different
They stay the same, as the system is always at equilibrium
They change only when the temperature is altered as well
They all change until equilibrium is reached again in the mixture

items.why: The system is no longer at equilibrium, and the concentrations of all the substances change until equilibrium is reached again.

items.stem: The forward reaction of a reversible reaction is endothermic. The temperature of the system at equilibrium is increased. What happens to the relative amount of products?

options.text: It increases, because the reaction is endothermic in the forward direction
It decreases, because raising the temperature will release more energy
It decreases, because the reactants are used up much more quickly
It stays the same, because heating changes only the reaction rates

items.why: The relative amount of products at equilibrium increases for an endothermic reaction when the temperature is increased.

items.stem: The forward reaction of a reversible reaction is exothermic. The temperature of the system at equilibrium is increased. What happens to the relative amount of products?

options.text: It increases, because the forward reaction is the exothermic one
It decreases, because the forward reaction gives out energy
It increases, since heating always improves any yield
It stays the same, since heating changes only the rates

items.why: The relative amount of products at equilibrium decreases for an exothermic reaction when the temperature is increased.

items.stem: The forward reaction of a reversible reaction is endothermic. The temperature of the system at equilibrium is decreased. What happens to the relative amount of products?

options.text: It increases, as cooling a mixture always drives the reaction onwards
It increases, as the system must give out energy when it cools down
It decreases, as the endothermic direction is no longer favoured
It stays the same, as cooling only slows both reactions down

items.why: The relative amount of products at equilibrium decreases for an endothermic reaction when the temperature is decreased.

items.stem: The forward reaction of a reversible reaction is exothermic. The temperature of the system at equilibrium is decreased. What happens to the relative amount of products?

options.text: It decreases, as a cooler mixture must form less product
It decreases, as the endothermic direction is favoured
It stays the same, as cooling alters only the two rates
It increases, as the forward reaction is exothermic

items.why: The relative amount of products at equilibrium increases for an exothermic reaction when the temperature is decreased.

items.stem: A sample of blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate is heated and turns white. What must be done to turn it blue again?

options.text: Nothing will work, as the direction is fixed once heating has started
Heat the white solid much more strongly for a longer period of time
Add water to the white solid, changing the conditions back again
Grind the white solid to a powder to raise its surface area

items.why: The direction of reversible reactions can be changed by changing the conditions; adding water reverses the change that heating produced.

items.stem: Ammonium chloride ⇌ ammonia + hydrogen chloride is given as an example of a reversible reaction. White ammonium chloride is heated in a tube and the two gases form. Which statement about this example is correct?

options.text: The ammonium chloride has been destroyed for good
Half of the solid always stays behind unchanged
The two gases must react first, before the solid heats
Cooling the gases re-forms ammonium chloride

items.why: The products react to produce the original reactant, which is what makes this the specification's example of a reversible reaction.

items.stem: Heating blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate to form white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate and water takes in 45 kJ of energy. Water is then added to the white solid. What happens to the energy?

options.text: Less than 45 kJ is given out, because some energy is lost as heat
45 kJ is taken in, because this change also needs energy
45 kJ is given out, as the same amount of energy is transferred
Most of the 45 kJ is given out, but some is always lost

items.why: The reverse reaction is exothermic and, as the specification states, the same amount of energy is transferred in each case.

items.stem: Why must a reversible reaction be carried out in apparatus that prevents reactants and products escaping if equilibrium is to be reached?

options.text: Escaped products cannot take part in reverse reactions
The reverse reaction happens anyway, whatever escapes
Equilibrium means nothing at all is allowed to move about
The reactants and products must be present in equal amounts

items.why: The reverse rate can only rise to match the forward rate if the products stay in the mixture, so escape prevents equilibrium.

items.stem: In a sealed flask N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g). The forward reaction is exothermic. More nitrogen is pumped into the flask at constant temperature. What is the qualitative prediction?

options.text: Less ammonia is present at the new equilibrium
More ammonia forms at the new equilibrium
The amount of ammonia present cannot change
Ammonia forms faster but its amount is fixed

items.why: Increasing the concentration of a reactant means more products are formed until equilibrium is reached again.

items.stem: For the equilibrium CH3COOH + C2H5OH ⇌ CH3COOC2H5 + H2O, more ethanol (C2H5OH) is added. What happens?

options.text: More products form until equilibrium is reached again in the flask
More reactants form, because ethanol was added to the reactant side
Nothing changes at all, since the total mass has not altered
The reaction speeds up but no extra ester is being formed

items.why: If the concentration of a reactant is increased, more products will be formed until equilibrium is reached again.

items.stem: In the equilibrium 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3, sulfur trioxide (SO3) is continuously removed from the mixture. What happens?

options.text: More reactants form, because there is now less product present
More reactants react until equilibrium is reached again
Nothing happens, because the system stays at equilibrium
The mixture ends up holding equal amounts of each one

items.why: If the concentration of a product is decreased, more reactants will react until equilibrium is reached again.

items.stem: For the gaseous equilibrium N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), the pressure is increased. Which way does the equilibrium position shift?

options.text: Towards nitrogen and hydrogen, the side with more molecules
Neither way, as pressure cannot alter this mixture
Towards the ammonia, the side with the fewer molecules
Towards the nitrogen, which has heavier molecules

items.why: An increase in pressure shifts the position towards the side with the smaller number of molecules: four on the left, two on the right.

items.stem: For the gaseous equilibrium 2SO3(g) ⇌ 2SO2(g) + O2(g), the pressure is decreased. Which way does the equilibrium position shift?

options.text: To the left, towards the side with just two gas molecules
Neither way, since the numbers of atoms are equal here
Neither way, as pressure changes only alter rates
To the right, the side with three molecules of gas

items.why: A decrease in pressure shifts the position towards the side with the larger number of molecules: two on the left, three on the right.

items.stem: A sealed flask holds an equilibrium mixture of hydrogen, iodine and hydrogen iodide: H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI. Extra hydrogen is injected and the flask is left until equilibrium is reached again. What is found?

options.text: Less HI, and more iodine than there was before
The same HI and the same iodine as before
More HI, and less iodine than there was
Only the hydrogen is now at a higher level than before

items.why: Increasing a reactant concentration forms more product, and forming more HI uses up some of the iodine.

items.stem: For 2NO2 ⇌ N2O4 the forward reaction is exothermic. A sealed tube of the mixture is placed in iced water and the brown colour of NO2 fades. What does this show?

options.text: Cooling has stopped both of the reactions in the sealed tube
Cooling has increased the relative amount of the product N2O4
Cooling has moved the equilibrium towards the reactant NO2
Cooling has slowed the forward reaction down only

items.why: Lowering the temperature increases the relative amount of products for an exothermic reaction, so the brown NO2 is used up.

items.stem: A student is given the equilibrium H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), all gases, and increases the pressure on the sealed vessel. What should the student predict?

options.text: No shift, as each side has two molecules
A shift to the right, towards the hydrogen iodide
A shift to the left, towards hydrogen and iodine
A shift to the side with the heavier molecules

items.why: The sides have equal numbers of gas molecules, so neither side is favoured by a change in pressure.
